# UNITED STATES v. LAMBORN (2025)
## United States Court of Appeals, Fourth Circuit.
United States of America, Plaintiff - Appellee, v. Tony Minh Le, a/k/a Sneaks, a/k/a Sneaky, a/k/a T, a/k/a Tiger, Defendant - Appellant.
The district court sentenced Joseph Lamborn, Young Yoo, and Peter Le ("Peter") to life imprisonment for a slew of offenses, which we'll discuss in more detail later. The district court also sentenced Tony Le ("Tony") to 312 months' imprisonment for racketeering conspiracy and drug conspiracy.
And Tony and Peter led Tiger Side and Club Tiger, respectively.
The fourth superseding indictment charged Tony with another crime: racketeering conspiracy.^3 Since drug conspiracy and racketeering conspiracy aren't the "same offense," the Double Jeopardy Clause didn't require the government to bring the racketeering charge earlier.
Finally, the absence of particularized prejudice weighs strongly against Tony.
While Tony asserted his speedy trial right, he didn't do so consistently.
Tony doesn't contest the 3,400 figure referenced in the report. So even if the district court attributed 500 grams of cocaine to Tony instead of 15 kilograms, it still would have assigned Tony the same base offense level.
The fourth superseding indictment also charged Tony with two counts of possessing a destructive device in furtherance of drug trafficking. But the jury acquitted Tony of those charges.

# United States v. Tony Tyrone Lee, A/K/A Antoine Sharrif Lee, A/K/A "Ant"
- **Court** Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
- **Docket number** 87-5589
- **Filed**
- **Precedential status** Unpublished
- **Citations** 1988 U.S. App. LEXIS 2087; 1988 WL 16939; 841 F.2d 1123

UNITED STATES of America, Plaintiff-Appellee,
v.
Tony Tyrone LEE, a/k/a Antoine Sharrif Lee, a/k/a "Ant",
Defendant-Appellant.
No. 87-5589.
United States Court of Appeals, Fourth Circuit.
Submitted: Dec. 30, 1987.
Decided: Feb. 23, 1988.

1
Tony Tyrone Lee appeals his convictions of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute and to distribute cocaine and marijuana (21 U.S.C. Sec. 846), possession of 195 grams of cocaine with intent to distribute (21 U.S. Sec. 841(a)(1)), and use of a communication facility to distribute cocaine and marijuana (21 U.S. Sec. 843(b)). Lee's counsel has filed a brief in accordance with Anders v. California, [386 U.S. 738](https://courtlistener.com/opinion/107423/anders-v-california/) (1967), indicating that, in his view, there are no meritorious issues for appeal. Lee has filed a supplemental pro se brief. In accordance with the requirements of [Anders, supra,](https://courtlistener.com/opinion/107423/anders-v-california/) we have examined the entire record in this case and find no meritorious issues for appeal. We briefly address the issues raised by counsel.

Finding no merit in these contentions, or in the supplemental arguments raised by Lee, and finding no error upon review of the record, we affirm the judgment of conviction. Pursuant to the plan adopted by the Fourth Circuit Judicial Council in implementation of the Criminal Justice Act of 1964, 18 U.S.C. Sec. 3006A, court-appointed counsel has the obligation to advise Lee of his right to petition the Supreme Court for a writ of certiorari and, if Lee desires him to do so, to prepare the necessary papers.

## Combined Opinion
```
UNPUBLISHED UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE FOURTH CIRCUIT UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, Plaintiff-Appellant, v. No. 96-4876 TONY LEONG, Defendant-Appellee. Appeal from the United States District Court for the District of Maryland, at Baltimore. Alexander Williams Jr., District Judge. (CR-96-272) Argued: May 5, 1997 Decided: June 26, 1997 Before WILKINS, Circuit Judge, Joseph F. ANDERSON, Jr., United States District Judge for the District of South Carolina, sitting by designation, and TRAXLER, United States District Judge for the District of South Carolina, sitting by designation.

_________________________________________________________________ OPINION PER CURIAM: Appellee Tony Leong ("Leong") was indicted for being a felon in possession of a firearm in violation of 18 U.S.C.A.§ 922(g) (West Supp. 1997). Prior to trial, Leong moved to suppress his statement admitting ownership of the firearm on the ground that the statement had been made in violation of Miranda v. Arizona ,
```
[384 U.S. 436](https://courtlistener.com/opinion/107252/miranda-v-arizona/)
```
(1966). The district court granted the motion to suppress and the Gov- ernment appealed pursuant to
```
18 U.S.C.A. § 3731
```
(West 1985). We affirm. I. On June 1, 1996 at approximately 3:00 a.m., United States Park Police Officer Matthew Nichols ("Nichols") observed a vehicle speeding on Maryland Route 197, a two-lane highway just off the Baltimore-Washington Parkway. Nichols activated his emergency equipment and the vehicle pulled to the side of the road. According to Nichols, the area where the stop occurred was dark, heavily wooded, and fairly isolated.

III. For the foregoing reasons, and under the narrow facts presented by this case, we affirm the decision of the district court suppressing the statement made by Leong. AFFIRMED

keenable.title: 4th Circuit largely upholds drug-gang murder convictions
keenable.snippet:
The [4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals](https://nclawyersweekly.com/tag/4th-u-s-circuit-court-of-appeals/?taxo-tag-body) affirmed most of the convictions arising from a violent Northern Virginia drug-trafficking enterprise, concluding that the jury reasonably found two defendants guilty of killing the victim while participating in a drug scheme. The court, however, vacated portions of several sentences after identifying discrepancies between the district court’s oral pronouncements and its written judgments.

Evaluating the record in the light most favorable to the government, the 4th Circuit held that a reasonable jury could conclude the two defendants knowingly participated in the plot to abduct the victim and remained present during the killing. Testimony indicated that one defendant supplied the weapon used in the stabbing and that both defendants continued with the plan even after being warned the victim would be shot. Those facts, the court said, supported the jury’s determination that the defendants shared the intent to murder while engaged in drug trafficking.
The court affirmed the convictions but vacated the sentences of three defendants after finding that their written judgments improperly added non-mandatory release conditions not announced at sentencing. The case returns to the U.S. District Court for resentencing.
The 37-page opinion is *United States v. Tony Minh Le*, Lawyers Weekly No. 001-178-25.

4th Circuit largely upholds drug-gang murder convictions

Listen to this article

The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed most of the convictions arising from a violent Northern Virginia drug-trafficking enterprise, concluding that the jury reasonably found two defendants guilty of killing the victim while participating in a drug scheme. The court, however, vacated portions of several sentences after identifying discrepancies between the district court’s oral pronouncements and its written judgments.

The appeal stemmed from a joint trial involving members of a group known as the Reccless Tigers, a gang involved in trafficking marijuana and cocaine and enforcing drug debts through intimidation and violence. According to the court, the gang operated through several interconnected cliques, with leaders and members assuming overlapping roles in drug distribution and enforcement.

The defendants challenged numerous convictions, but only one argument—relating to sentencing inconsistencies—had merit. Two of the defendants argued there was insufficient evidence to convict them of kidnapping conspiracy, kidnapping resulting in death, murder in aid of racketeering, and killing while engaged in drug trafficking. The court rejected these arguments.

Evaluating the record in the light most favorable to the government, the 4th Circuit held that a reasonable jury could conclude the two defendants knowingly participated in the plot to abduct the victim and remained present during the killing. Testimony indicated that one defendant supplied the weapon used in the stabbing and that both defendants continued with the plan even after being warned the victim would be shot. Those facts, the court said, supported the jury’s determination that the defendants shared the intent to murder while engaged in drug trafficking.

ultimate.title: 4th Circuit largely upholds drug-gang murder convictions
ultimate.snippet:
The [4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals](https://nclawyersweekly.com/tag/4th-u-s-circuit-court-of-appeals/?taxo-tag-body) affirmed most of the convictions arising from a violent Northern Virginia drug-trafficking enterprise, concluding that the jury reasonably found two defendants guilty of killing the victim while participating in a drug scheme. The court, however, vacated portions of several sentences after identifying discrepancies between the district court’s oral pronouncements and its written judgments.

Evaluating the record in the light most favorable to the government, the 4th Circuit held that a reasonable jury could conclude the two defendants knowingly participated in the plot to abduct the victim and remained present during the killing. Testimony indicated that one defendant supplied the weapon used in the stabbing and that both defendants continued with the plan even after being warned the victim would be shot. Those facts, the court said, supported the jury’s determination that the defendants shared the intent to murder while engaged in drug trafficking.
The court affirmed the convictions but vacated the sentences of three defendants after finding that their written judgments improperly added non-mandatory release conditions not announced at sentencing. The case returns to the U.S. District Court for resentencing.
The 37-page opinion is *United States v. Tony Minh Le*, Lawyers Weekly No. 001-178-25.
